design_detail: Cross-sectional PET study (Archives of General Psychiatry 2011;68:562-576) in Copenhagen comparing serotonin transporter binding ([11C]DASB, non-displaceable binding potential) and 5-HT2A receptor binding ([18F]altanserin, binding potential of specific binding) in 24 people who used MDMA and/or hallucinogens and 21 people who did not. The drug group was split by the ratio of lifetime exposures into 14 whose use was mainly MDMA and 10 whose use was mainly hallucinogens. Regions were drawn automatically on each person's MRI; the primary outcome was a volume-weighted neocortical average, with pallidostriatum, midbrain, amygdala and thalamus for the transporter. Dose-response and abstinence were examined within the drug group by regression on the logarithm of lifetime exposures and of days since last use, including a log-logistic model.
can_establish: That transporter binding was markedly lower in the group whose use was mainly MDMA than in both the hallucinogen-preferring group and the comparison group, that it was not lower in the hallucinogen-preferring group, that binding fell with the logarithm of lifetime MDMA tablets in every region except the midbrain, and that binding was higher in people whose last MDMA use was longer ago in subcortical regions but not in neocortex.
cannot_establish: That MDMA caused the reduction (cross-sectional, self-selected groups); that the subcortical relation with time since last use is recovery within a person (it compares different people, as the paper says); that the neocortex does not recover (a null in a noisy, low-binding region); or that the small cortical 5-HT2A difference is real, since it disappeared when two control outliers were removed.

sample.recruitment: Fliers, advertisements on relevant websites and word of mouth from other participants; face-to-face screening with drug-use questionnaires and the SCAN 2.1 psychiatric interview (pp. 562-563).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Aged 18-35, at least 12 lifetime exposures to MDMA or hallucinogens and use within the year before the scan; no drug use for 7 days before the scan. Comparison group excluded for more than 15 lifetime cannabis exposures or any other illicit drug use. Excluded for neurological or psychiatric disorders and any previous antidepressant or antipsychotic use (p. 563).
sample.demographics: Drug group 21 men and 3 women, mean age 24.6 (SD 4.0); comparison group 17 men and 4 women, 24.0 (3.4). The MDMA-preferring group had less education (p=0.04 across the three groups), started smoking earlier and smoked more (4.3 pack-years vs 1.0 in both other groups, p=0.02) (Table 1, p. 564; Table 3, p. 567).
sample.attrition: Altanserin data could not be quantified in 3 drug-group participants and 1 control because of a technical failure in blood metabolite analysis, leaving 21 and 20 for the receptor analysis (p. 564).
sample.selection_effects: Volunteers recruited through drug-related websites and word of mouth; group membership is defined after the fact by the ratio of MDMA to hallucinogen exposures, so the 'hallucinogen-preferring' group is also a group with lighter MDMA use (median 24 lifetime tablets) rather than an MDMA-naive group.

exposure.measurement: Copenhagen Substance Screening Questionnaire and modified Danish versions of the Customary Drinking and Drug Use Record and Lifetime Drinking History; urine screens every 2-3 days for the 7 days before scanning; gas chromatography-mass spectrometry of a 3.5-cm scalp hair segment covering about 3 months (pp. 563-564).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: MDMA-preferring group: median 635 calculated lifetime tablets (mean 1296, SD 1801, range 33-6590), 236 lifetime sessions, 3.3 use days a month, 4.3 tablets in a typical session, 268 mg of powder in a typical session, regular use for 72 months. Hallucinogen-preferring group: median 24 lifetime tablets (mean 60, range 6-362), 18 sessions, 0.3 use days a month, 1.8 tablets per session. Powder was converted to tablets by dividing milligrams by 60, the average Danish tablet content at the time (Table 1, p. 564; p. 563).
exposure.polysubstance: All 24 in the drug group had used cannabis; the MDMA-preferring group had used amphetamine and cocaine more recently and more often in the past 3 months (p=0.02 to 0.04); 9 of 14 had used GHB and 8 of 14 ketamine. Methamphetamine was not found in hair and is described as almost absent from the Danish market; cocaine is associated with higher, not lower, transporter binding (Table 1, p. 564; p. 573).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: At least 7 days with negative urine screens; actual time since last MDMA, median 44 days in the MDMA-preferring group (mean 57, SD 62, range 11-258) and 96 days in the hallucinogen-preferring group (mean 122, range 30-293) (Table 1, p. 564).

comparison.controls: 21 people of similar age and sex with at most 15 lifetime cannabis exposures and no other illicit drug use (p. 563).
comparison.matching: Age- and sex-matched by design; not matched on education or smoking, which differed.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No pre-use measurement; the paper considers and rejects a premorbid difference as less likely on the strength of animal experiments and the dose-response relation (p. 573), which is an argument, not a measurement.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Up to 15 lifetime cannabis exposures; no other illicit drugs; 4 of 21 were current smokers.

outcomes.instruments: [11C]DASB PET (90-min dynamic scan, multilinear reference tissue model MRTM2, cerebellum as reference) for the transporter; [18F]altanserin PET under steady-state conditions with arterial plasma for the 5-HT2A receptor; 3-T MRI for automatic region definition and grey-matter segmentation (pp. 564-565).
outcomes.validity_norms: [11C]DASB is selective for the serotonin transporter; the authors report published test-retest reliability for cortical regions (intraclass correlations 0.55-0.85) and note that cortical binding is low and noisy (p. 572). No normative values.
outcomes.operationalization: Serotonergic status is operationalized as regional binding potential; 'recovery' as a positive regression coefficient of binding on the logarithm of days since last MDMA use, across people.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Tukey correction for the three-group comparisons of the five transporter regions; the dose-response and abstinence regressions are reported uncorrected (pp. 565-566).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; region definition was automatic and model-based (p. 565).

analysis.effect_sizes: Group differences in transporter binding: pallidostriatum F=7.89, p=0.001; neocortex F=23.05, p<0.001; amygdala F=16.58, p<0.001; thalamus F=2.6, p=0.08; midbrain not significant. The MDMA-preferring group was lower than the comparison group by 19% in pallidostriatum, 32% in amygdala and 56% in neocortex (regionally 40% orbitofrontal to 73% occipital), with differences in binding-potential units of 0.30 (95% CI 0.09-0.50) in pallidostriatum, 0.15 (0.09-0.20) in neocortex and 0.49 (0.28-0.71) in amygdala; the hallucinogen-preferring group did not differ from controls. Dose-response within the drug group: a doubling of lifetime tablets corresponded to a fall in binding of 0.021 in neocortex (95% CI -0.029 to -0.014, p<0.001), 0.062 in pallidostriatum (-0.103 to -0.021, p=0.005), 0.067 in thalamus (p=0.006) and 0.075 in amygdala (p<0.001); no relation in midbrain. Abstinence: a doubling of days since last MDMA corresponded to higher binding of 0.14 in pallidostriatum (0.05-0.23, p=0.004), 0.12 in amygdala (0.04-0.21, p=0.008) and 0.11 in thalamus (0.002-0.22, p=0.046), with no relation in neocortex (0.005, -0.021 to 0.032, p=0.67); with adjustment for lifetime tablets the pallidostriatal (0.11, 0.02-0.19, p=0.02), amygdala (0.07, 0.01-0.14, p=0.02) and midbrain (0.10, 0.01-0.19, p=0.02) relations held and the thalamic one did not (p=0.17). From the log-logistic model, pallidostriatal binding in a person with the median lifetime use would reach the control average after an estimated 212 days (lower 95% limit 91 days; upper limit beyond a human lifespan). 5-HT2A receptor binding in the combined drug group was 9% lower in neocortex than in controls (medians 1.51 vs 1.66, Mann-Whitney p=0.03), but p=0.10 after excluding two controls with very high values, and the three-group comparison was not significant (p=0.07).
analysis.covariates: Age, body mass index, daylight minutes on the scan day, education and recent use of amphetamine, cocaine and cannabis were each tested as covariates; none was significant and none changed the group effects materially (p. 566).
analysis.selective_reporting: All five transporter regions and the receptor analyses are reported, including the null results in midbrain and in the hallucinogen-preferring group, and the sensitivity analysis that weakens the receptor finding.
analysis.power: Not reported. The groups are small (14, 10 and 21), and the paper notes that the cortical receptor reduction was modest and might be a power problem.

interpretation_gap.results_show: People whose drug use was mainly MDMA had markedly lower transporter binding than people who used mainly hallucinogens and than people who used neither, with a graded relation to lifetime tablets, and higher binding in those whose last use was longer ago in subcortical regions but not in neocortex; cortical 5-HT2A binding was slightly lower in the drug groups, a difference that did not survive the removal of two control outliers.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that MDMA but not hallucinogen use 'is associated with changes in the cerebral presynaptic serotonergic transmitter system', that the association is mediated by a direct presynaptic effect rather than by 5-HT2A agonism, and that the data suggest that subcortical, but not cortical, binding might recover after several months of abstinence (abstract, p. 562). The wording is careful: the paper explicitly declines to use the word neurotoxicity for its own data (p. 571) and states that the recovery calculation rests on comparisons between people rather than within them (p. 570). The mechanistic conclusion nonetheless rests on a comparison of two self-selected groups that also differ in amount and recency of every drug they used.

timeline.event: First [11C]DASB study, with the same cortical pattern but no subcortical reduction
Largest [11C]DASB study, cortical and hippocampal reductions with normal striatum
Independent study with arterial input: cortical reductions, no subcortical change, no relation with abstinence
No difference in men abstinent for at least a year
Review treats the subcortical relation with abstinence as part of the evidence that binding recovers over 40 to 200 days

replication.where_it_stands: The cortical reduction and the dose relation agree with the other [11C]DASB studies; this study is the only one of them to find a subcortical (pallidostriatal and amygdala) reduction, and the only one to find a positive relation between binding and time since last use, which the New York study with the same tracer did not.

funding.funder: Rigshospitalet, the Lundbeck Foundation, the Danish Medical Research Council, the H:S Research Council, the Sawmill owner Jeppe Juhl and Wife Ovita Juhls Foundation, and the John and Birthe Meyer Foundation (p. 574).
funding.affiliations_note: Neurobiology Research Unit, Copenhagen University Hospital Rigshospitalet; hair analyses by the Section of Forensic Chemistry, University of Copenhagen.

what_would_settle_it: Repeated scanning of the same people over a year or more of abstinence, with exposure verified in hair at each point, and a comparison group of people who use other drugs but not MDMA; that design would turn the between-person dose and abstinence relations into within-person change.

domains.note: The MDMA-preferring group smoked more, had less education and had used amphetamine and cocaine more recently; covariates were tested one at a time in small groups rather than adjusted jointly.

Hair analysis confirmed recent MDMA in 13 of 14 in the MDMA-preferring group and urine confirmed short-term abstinence, but lifetime tablet counts are self-reported, powder was converted to tablets by an average content, and the counts span two orders of magnitude.
Small self-selected groups defined after the fact by the ratio of their exposures; no pre-use measurement.
Receptor data missing for 4 of 45 because of a technical failure; transporter data complete.
Selective tracers and model-based quantification, but cortical transporter binding is low and noisy, and the receptor outcome is sensitive to two outlying control values.
Regional comparisons Tukey-corrected, null results and the fragile receptor finding reported in full.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A carefully analysed cross-sectional study whose main threats are its small, self-selected groups and their differences in other drug use; it can be cited for the group difference, for the graded relation to lifetime use, and for a between-person relation between binding and time since last use in subcortical regions, not for causation, for recovery within a person, or for the cortical 5-HT2A difference.

key_findings.finding: Transporter binding differed between the three groups in pallidostriatum (F=7.89, p=0.001), neocortex (F=23.05, p<0.001) and amygdala (F=16.58, p<0.001), with the thalamus borderline (F=2.6, p=0.08) and the midbrain unchanged.

Compared with the group that used neither drug, the MDMA-preferring group had binding lower by 19% in pallidostriatum, 32% in amygdala and 56% in neocortex (40% orbitofrontal, 47% parietal, 48% superior temporal, 51% medial inferior temporal, 53% medial inferior frontal, 61% superior frontal, 66% sensory-motor, 73% occipital); the hallucinogen-preferring group did not differ from controls in any region.
key_findings.locator: Results, 'SERT binding', 1st paragraph (continued p. 567); Figures 1 and 2
key_findings.note: The hallucinogen-preferring group had nonetheless used MDMA (median 24 lifetime tablets), so it is also a light-use group, as the paper notes (p. 571).

key_findings.finding: Binding fell with the logarithm of lifetime MDMA tablets in every region but the midbrain: a doubling of tablets corresponded to a fall of 0.021 binding-potential units in neocortex (95% CI -0.029 to -0.014, p<0.001), 0.062 in pallidostriatum (-0.103 to -0.021, p=0.005), 0.067 in thalamus (p=0.006) and 0.075 in amygdala (p<0.001).
key_findings.note: The printed intervals for thalamus (-0.113 to 0.022) and amygdala (-0.106 to 0.045) have positive upper limits that contradict their p-values; the minus signs appear to be missing (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Binding was higher in people whose last MDMA use was longer ago, in pallidostriatum (0.14 per doubling of days, 95% CI 0.05-0.23, p=0.004), amygdala (0.12, 0.04-0.21, p=0.008) and thalamus (0.11, 0.002-0.22, p=0.046), but not in neocortex (0.005, -0.021 to 0.032, p=0.67); after adjustment for lifetime tablets the pallidostriatal, amygdala and midbrain relations held and the thalamic one did not.
key_findings.note: This is a comparison between people scanned once, not a follow-up; the paper says so (p. 570).

key_findings.finding: From the log-logistic model, pallidostriatal binding in a person with the median lifetime use would be expected to reach the control average about 212 days after the last dose (lower 95% limit 91 days; the upper limit is beyond a human lifespan).
key_findings.note: The Comment rounds this to approximately 200 days (p. 570). The upper limit shows how weak the estimate is.

key_findings.finding: Cortical 5-HT2A receptor binding was 9% lower in the combined drug group than in controls (medians 1.51 vs 1.66, p=0.03), but the difference was no longer significant (p=0.10) when two controls with very high values were excluded, and the three-group comparison was not significant (p=0.07).
Neither the dose-response relation nor the abstinence relation appeared for hallucinogen use, and no relation was found between 5-HT2A binding and lifetime use or time since last use of either drug.
key_findings.locator: Results, 'SERT binding', last paragraph (p. 568); Results, 'Serotonin2A receptor binding' (p. 570)

key_findings.finding: Age, body mass index, daylight on the scan day, education and recent amphetamine, cocaine and cannabis use were tested as covariates one at a time and none was significant or changed the group effects.

reporting_issues.issue: The dose-response intervals printed for thalamus (-0.113 to 0.022) and amygdala (-0.106 to 0.045) include zero although the same sentence gives p=0.006 and p<0.001; the intervals for neocortex and pallidostriatum are printed with both limits negative.
reporting_issues.consequence: The upper limits are almost certainly missing a minus sign (-0.022, -0.045); as printed, two of the four dose-response results are internally inconsistent. Checked on the rendered page: the printed text matches the extraction.

reporting_issues.issue: The 5-HT2A outcome is defined in the Methods as the binding potential of specific binding (BPP) but is reported in the Results text as BPND.
reporting_issues.consequence: Mixed labels for the same measure; the values (medians 1.51 and 1.66) belong to the altanserin steady-state analysis described in the Methods.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 4 states that the partial residual plot is adjusted to a median lifetime use of 314 tablets, while Table 1 (p. 564) gives medians of 635 in the MDMA-preferring group and 24 in the hallucinogen-preferring group; the pooled median is not reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: The reader cannot check which group the 212-day estimate describes; it is an extrapolation from a between-person model in 24 people.

reporting_issues.issue: The thalamic group difference is reported as borderline (F=2.6, p=0.08) with a note that it became p=0.04 when one woman with no MDMA in hair was excluded.
reporting_issues.consequence: A single participant moves this result across the conventional threshold; the thalamic finding should not be counted as established.

reporting_issues.issue: The group labelled by preference for hallucinogens had itself used MDMA (median 24 lifetime tablets, 9 of 10 had used it), so the contrast between the two drug groups is not MDMA versus no MDMA but heavy versus light MDMA use.
reporting_issues.consequence: The mechanistic conclusion (that hallucinogen-type 5-HT2A agonism does not lower transporter binding) is supported, but the group labels overstate the contrast; the paper acknowledges this.

verification.source_read: PDF, pp. 562-576 (all pages; Tables 1-4 read in the extraction, the dose-response intervals on p. 568 checked on the rendered page; Figures 1-6 are images and no values were read from them)
